examples: I can only get to know him through his works.
There's no time, so the only option is to ask him.
Only 100 yen is left.
It's a limited-edition item you can only buy here.
I don't have time today, so I can only eat at a convenience store.
It's a secret that only he knows.
fields.explain:
しか comes after a noun/quantity/pronoun indicating a place, and before a negative verb.
Keep the relational particles before しか when needed:日本 でしか 見られ ない ,今日 までにしか でき ない .
Different from だけ: だけ is neutral, while しか has the nuance of “there is nothing else”.
V-辞書形+ しかない expresses reluctance.

• Limitation of scope: “only … and not … (there is nothing else)”.
• Stronger nuance than だけ: しか emphasizes a sense of lack/dissatisfaction.
• V-辞書形 + しかない has the idiomatic meaning “the only option is to …”.
• Must be used with the negative form (ない/ありません/できない…), not with the affirmative.
fields.notes:
• The subject is often omitted in conversation: これしかない（this is all there is）.
• With people/animals: ～しかいない is used very naturally: 会場にはスタッフしかいない。
• Emphasize the limitation with “たった/わずか + 数量 + しか + ない”.
mistakes: Using the affirmative with しか: 水しか飲む（wrong）→ 水しか飲まない.
Wrong particle position: 水をしか飲まない（extra を）→ 水しか飲まない.
Confusing it with “だれも～ない”: “だれしか～ない” is not used; the correct forms are だれもいない／彼しかいない.
Forgetting to keep the relational particle: ここしか買えない（ambiguous）→ ここでしか買えない.

fields.connection: V/A plain form + し / N・Na + だし
examples: It was far, and my luggage was heavy too, so I got tired.
Last night it was hot, and the neighbors were noisy too, so I couldn't sleep well.
fields.explain: ◎ 「し」, as used in「忙しいですし」or「お金もありません」, is used when stating one after another several things of the same kind.
fields.notes:
meaning_vi: Both… and…, and also…
explain: When persuading/giving reasons, put the strongest element at the end of the chain to lead to the conclusion.
In formal writing, the last one can be replaced with ～上に／さらに for better flow.
Avoid overusing し clauses in one long sentence.
examples: 1. このアプリは無料だし、使いやすいし、おすすめです。
This app is free and easy to use, so I recommend it.
2. 駅に近いし、静かだし、ここに住みたい。
It's close to the station and quiet, so I want to live here.
3. 今日は雨だし、寒いし、家にいよう。
It's raining today, and it's cold too, so let's stay home.
4. 時間もないし…また今度。
There's no time anyway… next time, then.
mistakes: Dropping だ with な形容詞/N: ×便利し → 便利だし.
Confusing it with ～て for giving reasons. The JLPT often requires choosing し when “multiple reasons” are needed.
Ending with し in formal written language can lack coherence if there is no clear conclusion.

fields.explain:
Often used with words indicating the number of times:一度／何回も／数回／一回も…ない to make clear how often the experience happened.
Polite form: 〜たことが あります ／〜たことが ありません .
When asking about experience: 〜たことが ありますか ？ is the polite, neutral pattern.

• Vたことがある expresses a past experience without a specific point in time, focusing on “whether one has ever done it or not”.
• Negative: Vたことがない = has never had that experience at all.
• Not used with very specific events/clear points in time (昨日/先週…), because that contradicts its “non-specific time” nature.
• Different from plain Vた: Vた tells of something that happened once (a time may be given); Vたことがある emphasizes the experience of having done it.
fields.notes:
• Adding a broad time frame is still fine: 子どものころに、海外へ行ったことがある (childhood, not a specific point in time).
• With もう/まだ: もう行ったことがあります (have already been)／まだ行ったことがありません (have still never been).
• In natural conversation, ことが is often omitted: 食べたことある？ (colloquial).
mistakes: Attaching a specific point in time: “昨日富士山に登ったことがある” (unnatural) → “昨日登った” or “富士山に登ったことがある”.
Confusing it with habit: “よく行く” ≠ “行ったことがある”. One is frequent, the other is an experience one has had.
Dropping こと is inappropriate in formal written language: “食べたことある” is colloquial; the JLPT requires the full form.
Incorrect double negative: “一度も行ったことありません” (correct), not “一度も行ったことないです” in standard exam language (keep the level of politeness consistent).

examples: You have to get up early tomorrow morning, so you'd better go to bed now.
It's better not to eat much before going to bed.
If you have a headache, you'd better go to bed early today.
I think you should talk to your boss about that matter.
It's better not to push yourself too hard at work.
Between English and Japanese, it's better to write in Japanese.
fields.explain:
Advice of a moderate degree, friendly; in polite contexts, ～ほうがよい/よろしいです can be used.
Avoid using it directly with superiors/customers unless asked; replace it with a soft suggestion: ～てはいかがでしょうか, ～たらいかがですか.
Not used for strict rules/norms (use ～べきだ/～ねばならない).

• Gives advice or a recommendation that is personal/based on experience.
• Affirmative: V-たほうがいい; Negative: V-ないほうがいい (more common than V-なかったほうがいい).
• V-るほうがいい is used for an objective comparison of two options, not necessarily direct advice.
• Strength: ～たほうがいい < ～べきだ (strong, normative) / softer: ～たらどう/～たらいい.
• Usually used in the present tense; the implied subject is “you/I/we”.
fields.notes:
• In conversation, add よ/ね/よね to adjust the degree of familiarity and certainty.
• Avoid V-なかったほうがいい (unnatural); use V-ないほうがいい.
• With nouns/choices, use ～にしたほうがいい to recommend a choice: Aにしたほうがいい。
mistakes: Using V-るほうがいい as general advice → for positive advice, prefer V-たほうがいい.
Using it with a subject that does not fit the social context (speaking directly to a superior) → not polite enough.
Confusing it with ～べきだ: when the question calls for a soft recommendation, choose ～たほうがいい.

examples: I run every day for my health.
I'm studying hard so that I can become a doctor in the future.
I just can't memorize kanji. So, to memorize them, I'm practicing by writing them over and over.
My father works hard for our family.
This is a dictionary for people who study Japanese.
I don't want to work for the company. I work for myself.
fields.notes:
Note:
「ために」の前に,可能形、ナイ形など使えない。
The potential form or the ない-form of a verb cannot be used before 「ために」。
1.  X日本語が話せるために、毎日練習します。　→日本語が話せるように～
X To be able to speak Japanese, I practice every day. → To be able to speak Japanese…
2.  X　かぜをひかないために、注意してください。　→　かぜをひかないように～(→　N3)
X To not catch a cold, please be careful. → To not catch a cold…
◎ A sentence pattern expressing cause or reason. Used with the plain form of verbs and「N＋の」.
1. かぜを 引いたため、昨日は 休みました。
I caught a cold, so I took yesterday off.
2. 大雪の ため、電車が 止まって います。
The trains have stopped because of heavy snow.
More formal than ので/から when stating a cause; often used in announcements, signs, and the news.
For purpose, it is more formal than ～ように; suitable when the verb is volitional and there is a specific goal.
Do not use ために (purpose) with non-volitional/potential verbs such as分かる、見える、起きる… (switch to ～ように).
1. A:　なんの　ために　貯金していますか。
B:　将来　自分の店を　持つために、貯金しています。
A: What are you saving money for?
B: I'm saving money so that I can have a shop of my own in the future.
2. A:　健康の　ために、　何か　していますか。
B:　いいえ。でも、来週から　毎朝　走ろうと。
A：Do you do anything for your health?
B: No. But starting next week, I'm planning to go running every morning.
3. 家族の　ために、うちを　建てます。
I'm going to build a house for my family.
──────
1. 日本に留学するために、日本語を勉強している。
I'm stud

fields.meaning: Should V ~ | It would be good if…
examples: If you're tired, you should rest a little.
I wish I could work in Japan.
What should I do about this problem?
I wish the rain would stop.
It would be nice if we had time, wouldn't it?
We should have asked for advice sooner, shouldn't we?
fields.explain:
Gives light, polite advice: Vたらいいですよ／と思います。
For wishes, add な(あ)/のに to heighten the emotion:会えたらいいな／雨ならやんだらいいのに。
Asking for an opinion: どうしたらいいですか／いつ行っ たらいいですか。
Should not be used directly with superiors when it risks sounding like a command; use softer patterns such as ～ていただけますか or ～たらいかがですか.

• Advice/suggestion: “It would be good to …” → softer than 〜たほうがいい, suited to lightly polite communication.
• Personal wish: “If only/I wish …” → used with な(あ)/ね to express feeling: 会えたらいいな。
• Asking how to deal with something: “どうしたらいいですか” is a fixed pattern for asking for advice.
• The たら condition means “it would be good if that condition happened” (supposition/possibility).
fields.notes:
• “〜たらいいのに” often expresses regret or a desire that is hard to fulfill.
• When asking for instructions, “どうしたらいいですか” is more natural than “どうすればいいですか” in spoken language; both are correct.
• Don't use “〜たらいい！” as a command; add ですよ/と思います to soften it.
meaning_vi: It would be good if… / should…
explain: Light advice, less imposing than ～べきだ or ～ほうがいい.
The question form “～ばいいですか” is commonly used when you want the listener to show you how to solve something.
～ばいいのに carries a feeling of reproach/regret; be careful using it with older people/superiors.
～ばよい is formal/very polite, used in written language and at work.
examples: 1. 疲れたら、休めばいい。
When you get tired, just rest.
2. 「駅はどう行けばいいですか」「この道をまっすぐいけばいいですよ」
"How do I get to the station?" "Just go straight along this road and you'll get there."
──────
1. どうすればいいですか。
What should I do?
2. 迷ったら、先生に聞けばいい。
If you're unsure, just ask the teacher.
3. そんなに心配しなければいい。
You don't need to worry that much.
4. もっと勉強すればいいのに。
You should study more (you really ought to).
5. 雨なら、無理に行かなければいい。
If it rains, you don't have to go.
6. 今回は謝ればいいだけだ。
This time, all you need to do is apologize.
comparison: Pattern | Nuance | Difference | Short example
～ばいい | Light advice/sufficient condition | Soft, not forcing | 早（はや）く寝（ね）れ ばいい。
～たらいい | Equivalent, natural in spoken language | Hypothetical, after the condition happens | 早（はや）く寝（ね）たらいい。
～ほうがいい | Stronger advice | Compares 2 options, clearly implies “should” | 早（はや）く寝（ね）たほうがいい。
～べきだ | Obligation/norm | Strong, based on principle | 守（まも）るべきだ。
～てもいい | Permission | Not advice; it is permission | 帰（かえ）ってもいい。
common_mistakes: • Misreading it as a command: ～ばいい does not mean “must”; it is only a light suggestion.
• Confusing it with ～てもいい (permission) → different function.
• Wrong ば形 conjugation of godan verbs: 書く→書けば; 買う→買えば; 行く→行けば.
• Wrong nuance: for a strong suggestion, choose ～ほうがいい／～べきだ instead of ～ばいい.
explain: ～Vば いいです： Should V ~
Used to ask for or give advice.
Usage is the same as NVTたら　いいです。
examples: 1. A:　本を　借りたいんですが、どう　すれば　いいですか。
B:　受付で　カードを　作って　もらって　ください。
A: I'd like to borrow a book. What should I do?
B: Please have a card made at the reception desk.
2. A:　友達が　結婚します。どんな物を　あげれば　いいですか。
B:　ワインを　あげれば　いいですよ。
A: My friend is getting married. What kind of thing should I give ?
B: Wine would be good.
explain: For your own wishes: ～といい んですが / のですが (polite, with a slight sense of worry).
For other people: ～といい ですね (polite, as a well-wish).
Giving advice: ～といい ですよ / よ (casual). Can be replaced with ～たらいい／～ばいい.
The content should be a future event; for the past, use ～とよかった (how nice it would have been) to express regret.
examples: 1. 試験、うまくいくといいですね。
I hope your exam goes well.
2. 忘れ物が見つかるといいんですが。
I hope the lost item turns up.
3. 時間があるといいね、映画に行こう。
I hope we have time. Let's go see a movie.
4. 風邪なら、今日は早く休むといいですよ。
If it's a cold, you should rest early today.
5. 英語は毎日少しずつ続けるといいよ。
With English, it's good to keep at it a little every day.
6. 明日は晴れだといいなあ。
I hope it's sunny tomorrow.
──────
1. ①いい仕事が見つかるといいですね。
I hope you find a good job.
2. ②運動会の日、雨が降らないといいですけど｡｡｡
I hope it doesn't rain on the day of the sports festival.
3. ③のどが痛いの？悪いかぜでないといいけど｡｡｡
Do you have a sore throat? I hope it's not a bad cold.
4. ④部屋がもっと広いといいけどなあ。
I wish the room were bigger.
5. ⑤ホームステイの家族がみんな親切だといいなあ。
I hope everyone in my homestay family is kind.
comparison: Pattern | Function | Difference | Short example
～といい（ですね） | Well-wishing/hope | For other people; polite. | 合格（ごうかく）だ といいですね。
～といい（んですが） | Hope (for oneself) | With a nuance of longing and worry. | 雨（あめ）がやむ といいんですが。
～たらいい／～ばいい | Suggestion | Similar to advice; sometimes more direct. | 休（やす）ん だらいい よ。
～ますように | Prayer/wish | More formal, leaning toward prayer. | 合格（ごうかく）し ますように。
～といい vs ～たい | Wish/hope vs desire | ～たい is the speaker's volition; ～といい is hoping for something beyond one's control. | 休（やす）み たい ／休（やす）み だといい。
common_mistakes: • Using ～といいです for your own wishes sounds stiff; more natural: ～といいんですが。
• Using ～といい to give overly direct advice in formal contexts; consider ～たらいかがでしょうか。
• Using ～といい for something fully under your own control → unnatural (×「早く寝るといいんですが」). Use ～ばいい／～たほうがいい instead。
• Confusing it with ～ますように (prayer). The JLPT tests the politeness nuance and the target (oneself vs other people).
meaning_vi: 「～ことを望んでいる。」 ～には話者自身の意志的行為を表す言葉は来ない。
I hope ~.
~ is not a word expressing a volitional act of the speaker themselves.
examples: 1. 疲れているようですね。あしたはゆっくり休むといいですよ。
You seem tired. You should take a good rest tomorrow.
2. その仕事、気が進まないのなら引き受けなければいいんじゃないですか。
If you don't feel like doing that job, why not just turn it down?
3. 申込書の書き方がわからなければ、事務の人に聞いてみたらいいですよ。
If you don't know how to fill out the application form, try asking someone in the office.
──────
1. 先生「このクラスも今日でお別れです。いつかまたみんなで会えるといいですね。」
Teacher「Today is also the day we say goodbye to this class. I hope we can all meet again someday.」
2. 最近ずっと体の調子が悪い。悪い病気でなければいいが…。
I haven't been feeling well for a while now. I hope it's nothing serious….
3. あした入学試験だ。頑張ろう。合格できたらいいなあ。
Tomorrow is the entrance exam. Let's do our best. I hope I can pass.
meaning_vi: Expresses advice or a suggestion.
（～ばいい）／（～たらいい）／（～と）+いい
examples: 1. ①　買えばいい／買ったらいい／買うといい
You should buy it.
2. ②　「日本語がうまくなるには、どうしたらいいですか。」
「日本人(にほんじん)と友達(ともだち)になるといいですよ。」
"What should I do to get better at Japanese?"
"You should make friends with Japanese people."
3. ③    勉強したくないなら、学校をやめればいい。
If you don't want to study, you should just quit school.
4. ➃　食べたくないなら、食べなければいい。
If you don't want to eat, you don't have to.
meaning_vi: I wish…, if only… it would be good (といい/たらいい)
mistakes: Confusing the “advice” function with the “wish” function: judge by the context and the sentence ending (ですよ vs な/のに).
Too direct with superiors → not polite enough; consider ～たらいかがですか/～ていただけますか.
Confusing it with 〜たほうがいい (stronger) in advice sentences in sensitive situations.

Spoken language, more direct than たらいい

examples: If you ask him, he'll probably know.
Tanaka and the others have probably already arrived in Tokyo.
It will probably snow tomorrow.
He has probably already gotten home.
That kind of plan probably won't work.
You think so too, right?
fields.explain:
Casual speech/male speech: ～だろう／～だろ？; polite style: ～でしょう／～でしょうか.
Combined with adverbs of conjecture: おそらく／たぶん ～だろう (raising/lowering the degree of certainty).
Avoid ～だろうですか. A polite question must be ～でしょうか.

• Conjecture with a moderate degree of confidence: “probably/ must be”.
• Used as a confirmation tag/a tag seeking agreement (especially in male speech): ～だろう？ “right?”.
• ～だろうか: wondering to oneself, deliberating; formal written language often uses ～であろう/～であろうか.
• More direct, stronger nuance than でしょう. In polite conversation, use でしょう.
fields.notes:
• Formal written form: ～であろう (same meaning, elevated style).
• Negative question: ～ないだろうか often means “isn't it the case that …?”.
• In polite communication, switch to ～でしょう to avoid sounding rough. | Variant: （～だろう）と思う — the speaker's conjecture
mistakes: Wrong form: × 静かだだろう → 静かだろう.
Mixing styles: × でしょうだろう (mixed up). Choose one consistent style.
Using だろうか for a polite question to a superior can sound somewhat stiff; prefer でしょうか.
Confusing its degree of certainty with ～かもしれない in trick questions about confidence level.

fields.meaning:
「～と言っている・～と聞いた。」「～と」のくだけた話し言葉で。②③④⑤のように、後の動詞（言っている・聞いたなど）をよく省略する。④のように、言った言葉に直接「って」をつけることもある。
Says that ~ / I heard that ~.
This is a word used in spoken language, a colloquial variant of ～と.
In examples ②③④, the verb that follows, いっている／きいた…, is often omitted.
In some cases, って is attached directly to the exact words that were said, as in example ④.
examples: "Mom, Dad says he'll be late today."
"Did Tanaka say they're going?" "No, they said they're not going."
"I learned this at school: apparently this area used to be sea a long time ago."
"What did the weather forecast say?" "It said it'll be sunny. And hot, too."
I got an email from Tei for the first time in ages. Tei says everything's fine.
Ogawa said they're taking today off.
fields.explain: A casual way of passing on hearsay or what someone else said (“I heard…/they said…”). Used a lot in conversation.
fields.notes:
1) Easily confused with the quotation particle と.
→ ～って is the colloquial form of と言って／という, used to report what was said/information.
2) Pay attention to the spoken-language context.
→ Often appears in conversation; not preferred in formal written language.
3) The two usages are easily confused.
→ It can mean “I heard…” or “they said…” (quoting), depending on the sentence.
